blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this NDSS'19 paper as a deep dive into secret leakage in public GitHub repositories, going beyond merely observing the problem to provide a longitudinal analysis, root cause insights, and limitations of existing mitigations. He emphasizes the paper's actionable findings, such as the effectiveness of pre-commit hooks using the paper's regex patterns (far superior to tools like TruffleHog at the time) and the critical need for immediate revocation of leaked secrets. The blog underscores the alarming speed at which secrets are discovered (median 20 seconds) and their persistence (81% remain after 16 days), even after history rewriting. Colyer motivates the paper by showing how even high-value targets and experienced developers leak secrets, and provides practical detection strategies using GitHub's APIs or BigQuery dataset.
paper_title: How Bad Can It Git? Characterizing Secret Leakage in Public GitHub Repositories
paper_abstract: —GitHub and similar platforms have made public collaborative development of software commonplace. However, a problem arises when this public code must manage authentication secrets, such as API keys or cryptographic secrets. These secrets must be kept private for security, yet common development practices like adding these secrets to code make accidental leakage frequent. In this paper, we present the first large-scale and longitudinal analysis of secret leakage on GitHub. We examine billions of files collected using two complementary approaches: a nearly six-month scan of real-time public GitHub commits and a public snapshot covering 13% of open-source repositories. We focus on private key files and 11 high-impact platforms with distinctive API key formats. This focus allows us to develop conservative detection techniques that we manually and automatically evaluate to ensure accurate results. We find that not only is secret leakage pervasive — affecting over 100,000 repositories — but that thousands of new, unique secrets are leaked every day. We also use our data to explore possible root causes of leakage and to evaluate potential mitigation strategies. This work shows that secret leakage on public repository platforms is rampant and far from a solved problem, placing developers and services at persistent risk of compromise and abuse. While this problem is known, it remains unknown to what extent secrets are leaked and how attackers can efficiently and effectively extract these secrets. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive, longitudinal analysis of secret leakage on GitHub. We build and evaluate two different approaches for mining secrets: one is able to discover 99% of newly committed files containing secrets in real time, while the other leverages a large snapshot covering 13% of all public repositories, some dating to GitHub’s creation.
